resources.title: Key verb tables
resources.summary: The four verbs you use most, être, avoir, aller and faire, in the present tense, and the three patterns regular verbs follow, with how the same verbs look in the other tenses.

sources.name: Pearson Edexcel GCSE French vocabulary and grammar guide

blocks.body: **How to read the tables.** Each row is one person: *je*, I (*j'* before a vowel); *tu*, you, to one person you know well; *il / elle / on*, he, she, and *on* for "one" or "we"; *nous*, we; *vous*, you, to a group or to an adult you do not know well; *ils / elles*, they. The **infinitive** is the form in the dictionary, such as *jouer*, to play. The **stem** is what is left when the ending comes off: *jou-*. A **past participle** is the form that follows *avoir* or *être* in the perfect tense: *joué*, played.

visual.alt: The verb être in the present, an irregular verb: je suis, tu es, il / elle / on est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils / elles sont

blocks.caption: **être**, to be. It is also the helper verb for the perfect tense (the past: *je suis allé(e)*, I went) of a short list of verbs, mostly about coming and going, such as *aller*, *venir*, *arriver*, *partir*, *rester* and *tomber*, and of every reflexive verb. Most verbs of movement, such as *marcher* and *courir*, still take *avoir*: *j'ai marché*, I walked.

visual.alt: The verb avoir in the present, an irregular verb: j'ai, tu as, il / elle / on a, nous avons, vous avez, ils / elles ont

blocks.caption: **avoir**, to have. The helper verb for the perfect tense of most verbs: *j'ai joué*, I played. It also appears in phrases where English uses *be*: *j'ai faim*, I am hungry; *j'ai quinze ans*, I am fifteen.

visual.alt: The verb aller in the present, an irregular verb: je vais, tu vas, il / elle / on va, nous allons, vous allez, ils / elles vont

blocks.caption: **aller**, to go. With an infinitive after it, it makes the near future: *je vais jouer*, I am going to play.

visual.alt: The verb faire in the present, an irregular verb: je fais, tu fais, il / elle / on fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils / elles font

blocks.caption: **faire**, to do or to make, and the weather: *il fait beau*, it is fine.

visual.alt: The verb jouer in the present, stem jou with the endings added: je joue, tu joues, il / elle / on joue, nous jouons, vous jouez, ils / elles jouent

blocks.caption: **Regular -er verbs**, the biggest group, shown with *jouer*, to play. Take off *-er* to leave the stem, *jou-*, and add these endings: *je joue*, I play or I am playing.

visual.alt: The verb choisir in the present, stem chois with the endings added: je choisis, tu choisis, il / elle / on choisit, nous choisissons, vous choisissez, ils / elles choisissent

blocks.caption: **Regular -ir verbs**, like *choisir*, to choose, and *finir*, to finish. Take off *-ir* and add these endings: *je choisis*, I choose. Not every *-ir* verb follows *choisir*: *partir*, *venir* and *ouvrir* each have a pattern of their own.

visual.alt: The verb entendre in the present, stem entend with the endings added: j'entends, tu entends, il / elle / on entend, nous entendons, vous entendez, ils / elles entendent

blocks.caption: **Regular -re verbs**, like *entendre*, to hear, and *vendre*, to sell. Take off *-re* and add these endings: *j'entends*, I hear. The *il*, *elle* and *on* form has no ending at all: *il entend*, he hears. *Prendre* and *traduire* have patterns of their own.

blocks.title: The same four verbs in other tenses, je form
rows: *j'ai été*: I was, I have been
*j'étais*: I was, I used to be
*j'ai eu*: I had, I have had
*j'avais*: I had, I used to have
*je suis allé(e)*: I went, I have gone
*j'allais*: I used to go, I was going
*je faisais*: I used to do, I was doing
*je ferai*: I will do, I will make
blocks.note: The future tense is Higher tier. In the perfect, *aller* takes *être*, so its past participle agrees with the person: *il est allé*, he went; *elle est allée*, she went. That is what *allé(e)* means: a girl adds the *e*.

blocks.title: The three regular patterns in other tenses, je form
blocks.note: The past participle swaps the infinitive ending: *-er* becomes *-é*, *-ir* becomes *-i*, *-re* becomes *-u*. The future tense is Higher tier, and there the specification asks for it only with *-er* verbs and with *aller*, *avoir*, *être* and *faire*.

applications.title: Talking about yourself
applications.body: Most of a speaking exam runs on these four: *je suis*, I am; *j'ai*, I have; *je vais*, I go; *je fais*, I do. With them in three tenses you can describe last weekend, today and next summer.

applications.title: Signs and weather forecasts
applications.body: Visiting France you will read *nous sommes ouverts*, we are open, on a shop door, and hear *il fait chaud*, it is hot, in a weather forecast: the verbs on this page, in the forms people actually use.

resources.title: Tense timeline
resources.summary: Every tense in the specification on one timeline, from the past to the future: when to use it, how it is made, and an example, most with a time phrase that signals the tense.

blocks.title: From the past to the future
rows: one finished action in the past
*avoir* or *être* in the present, plus a past participle
*hier, j'ai joué au foot*: yesterday I played football
what used to happen, what was going on, and descriptions in the past
the present *nous* form without *-ons*, plus *-ais, -ais, -ait* for *je, tu, il*. The plural endings *-ions, -iez, -aient* are Higher tier. *Être* alone starts from *ét-*: *j'étais*
*quand j'étais petit(e), je jouais au parc*: when I was little I used to play in the park
the stem plus the present endings: *jou-* plus *-e* gives *je joue*
*maintenant, je joue au tennis*: now I am playing tennis
*aller* in the present, plus an infinitive
*ce soir, je vais jouer*: this evening I am going to play
for *-er* verbs, the infinitive plus *-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont*. Four verbs have a stem of their own: *j'irai*, *j'aurai*, *je serai*, *je ferai*
*l'année prochaine, je jouerai*: next year I will play
the future stem plus the imperfect endings: *jouer* plus *-ais* gives *je jouerais*, I would play
*je voudrais jouer*: I would like to play
blocks.note: At Foundation tier the conditional is only *je voudrais*, *tu voudrais*, *il voudrait*: I, you, he would like. The imperative gives orders: *tourne à gauche*, turn left, to a friend; *tournez à gauche* to an adult or a group.

blocks.body:
**Build one sentence in each tense.** Start from *jouer au tennis*, to play tennis.

**Perfect.** *Avoir* in the present, *j'ai*, plus the past participle. For an *-er* verb swap *-er* for *-é*: *joué*. *Hier, j'ai joué au tennis*: yesterday I played tennis.

**Imperfect.** Take *nous jouons*, remove *-ons* to leave *jou-*, add *-ais*. *Je jouais au tennis*: I used to play tennis.

**Present.** Remove *-er* to leave *jou-*, add *-e*. *Je joue au tennis*: I play tennis, or I am playing tennis.

**Near future.** *Aller* in the present, *je vais*, plus the infinitive. *Demain, je vais jouer au tennis*: tomorrow I am going to play tennis.

**Future (Higher).** The infinitive plus *-ai*. *Je jouerai au tennis*: I will play tennis.

**Conditional (Higher).** The infinitive plus *-ais*. *Je jouerais au tennis*: I would play tennis.

**Aim for three time frames in every longer answer.** The longer writing questions and the speaking conversation ask you to refer to past, present and future events. Plan one sentence about the past, one about now and one about the future, and open each with a time phrase.

applications.title: A speaking answer that scores
applications.body: Asked about holidays: *l'année dernière, je suis allé(e) en Espagne*, last year I went to Spain (perfect); *normalement, je reste en France*, usually I stay in France (present); *l'année prochaine, je vais visiter l'Italie*, next year I am going to visit Italy (near future). Three tenses in three sentences.

applications.title: Telling a story
applications.body: French stories mix two past tenses: the imperfect sets the scene, *il faisait beau*, the weather was fine, and the perfect moves the action on, *soudain, j'ai vu un chien*, suddenly I saw a dog.

resources.title: Question words and connectives
resources.summary: The question words, time phrases and connectives that turn short answers into developed ones, all from the specification's vocabulary list.

sources.name: Pearson Edexcel GCSE French vocabulary and grammar guide

blocks.title: Question words
rows: how much, how many? With time: how long?
turns a statement into a question
blocks.note: *Quel* agrees with the noun after it: *quel sport ?*, which sport?; *quelle ville ?*, which town?; *quels films ?*, which films?; *quelles chansons ?*, which songs? *Que* and *quoi* both mean what: *que* comes first, *que fais-tu ?*, and *quoi* comes last, *tu fais quoi ?* Both ask: what are you doing? *Que* becomes *qu'* before a vowel.

blocks.title: Three ways to ask the same question
rows: Say the statement and raise your voice
where do you want to go?
where do you want to go?
Swap the verb and the person
where do you want to go?
blocks.note: With no question word the first two ways still work: *tu aimes le sport ?* and *est-ce que tu aimes le sport ?* both mean: do you like sport? *Est-ce que* becomes *est-ce qu'* before a vowel: *quand est-ce qu'il vient ?*, when is he coming?

blocks.title: Connectives
blocks.note: Words marked Higher are in the Higher tier list only. You may still use them at Foundation. *Ou* with no accent is or; *où* with an accent is where. *Parce que* becomes *parce qu'* before a vowel: *parce qu'il pleut*, because it is raining.

blocks.title: Time phrases, and the tense they signal
rows: near future, or future at Higher
near future, or future at Higher
near future, or future at Higher
blocks.note: A time phrase points to a time, not to one tense. *Hier* goes with the perfect for an event, *hier, j'ai joué au foot*, yesterday I played football, and with the imperfect for a description, *hier, il faisait beau*, yesterday the weather was fine. *Souvent* and *toujours* also work in the past: *je jouais souvent au parc*, I often used to play in the park.

applications.title: Developing a speaking answer
applications.body: Asked *tu aimes le sport ?*, do you like sport?, answer, give a reason and add a contrast: *oui, j'aime le foot parce que c'est rapide, mais je n'aime pas le rugby*: yes, I like football because it is fast, but I do not like rugby.

applications.title: Understanding a listening question
applications.body: The listening questions are set in English, so match each English question word to the French you will hear. A question that asks why means you are waiting for *parce que* or *car*, because. One that asks when means a time phrase such as *hier* or *demain*. In the speaking exam the teacher asks in French: *pourquoi ?* is your cue to answer with *parce que*.
